notes.title: Positional number systems
notes.body: In base b, each digit counts powers of b. Worked example: 173 in binary. 173 = 128+32+8+4+1 = 2^7+2^5+2^3+2^2+2^0, so 173₁₀ = **10101101**₂ (verify: int('10101101',2) = 173). In hex, group bits in fours: 10101101 → AD, so 173₁₀ = **0xAD**. Octal/hex exist to make binary readable: one hex digit is exactly 4 bits, one octal digit exactly 3.

notes.title: Two's complement
notes.body: Signed integers use two's complement: negate by flipping bits and adding 1. Worked example: represent -42 in 8 bits. 42 = 00101010; flip → 11010101; +1 → **11010110**. Check: 11010110₂ as unsigned = 214; 214 − 256 = **-42** ✓. Range of 8-bit two's complement: −128..127. The top bit is the sign bit; overflow wraps silently — the source of countless bugs.

notes.title: Bitwise operations, computed
notes.body: Worked with a=0b11001100 (204), b=0b10101010 (170): a AND b = 0b10001000 = **136**; a OR b = 0b11101110 = **238**; a XOR b = 0b01100110 = **102**; NOT a (8-bit) = **51**. Shifts: 204 << 2 = **816** (×4); 204 >> 2 = **51** (÷4, floor). Masks isolate fields: x & 0x0F keeps the low nibble. Flags, permissions, and subnet masks are all bit patterns manipulated exactly this way.

notes.title: Subnet math with real computation
notes.body: Worked example: 192.168.10.0/26, computed with Python's ipaddress module. Addresses total: 2^(32−26) = 2^6 = **64**. Network: **192.168.10.0**; broadcast: **192.168.10.63**; usable: 64 − 2 = **62**; range 192.168.10.1 – 192.168.10.62; mask: **255.255.255.192**. Never hand-compute what the ipaddress module verifies: write the plan, then assert every address with code. Every address, mask, and permission bit in the modules below is computed exactly this way.

notes.title: Parity and checksums
notes.body: Error detection starts with parity: count the 1-bits; even parity appends 0 if the count is even, 1 if odd. Worked example: byte 0b11001100 has **4** one-bits (even), so the even-parity bit is **0**. Checksums generalize this: the IPv4 header checksum is the one's-complement sum of 16-bit words. These are the simplest instances of the integrity machinery (hashing, CRCs) used everywhere in systems work.

notes.title: Fixed-width pitfalls
notes.body: Computers compute in fixed widths, and the width is part of the answer. Worked examples: (200 + 100) mod 256 = **44** in 8-bit unsigned arithmetic — silent wraparound. In two's complement 8-bit, 127 + 1 = **-128** (−128): signed overflow. Shifting 1 left by 31 in 32-bit signed gives the most negative number. Rule: know your width, know your signedness, and test the boundaries 0, max, max+1, −1 explicitly.

notes.title: Propositions and truth values
notes.body: A proposition is a statement that is either true or false, never both. `p AND q` is true only when both are true; `p OR q` is true when at least one is true; `NOT p` flips the value. Worked example: evaluate `(p AND q) OR (NOT r)` at p=T, q=F, r=T. First `p AND q` = T AND F = F. Then `NOT r` = NOT T = F. Finally `F OR F` = **F**. So the whole expression is **F**. Work inside-out: parentheses first, then NOT, then AND, then OR — the same precedence habit that prevents bugs in code conditions.

notes.title: Truth tables, computed by enumeration
notes.body: A truth table lists every assignment of the variables. With n variables there are 2^n rows — for n=3 that is **8** rows, computed as 2^3. Worked example: the implication `p -> q`, defined as `(NOT p) OR q`. Its table: p=T,q=T -> T; p=T,q=F -> F; p=F,q=T -> T; p=F,q=F -> T. The only false row is true-premise/false-conclusion. Enumerating all rows mechanically (as the lab does in Python) removes all doubt: no case is forgotten, because the count 2^n proves the table is complete.

notes.title: De Morgan's laws, verified by brute force
notes.body: De Morgan's laws: `NOT (p AND q)` equals `(NOT p) OR (NOT q)`, and `NOT (p OR q)` equals `(NOT p) AND (NOT q)`. Worked verification: checking all 4 assignments of (p,q) in Python, every row agrees — **True**. This is the law behind simplifying negated conditions: `NOT (admin AND active)` becomes `NOT admin OR NOT active`. In code and in firewall/policy rules, pushing NOT inward with De Morgan turns an unreadable negated conjunction into a plain disjunction.

notes.title: Implication and the contrapositive
notes.body: `p -> q` (if p then q) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive `(NOT q) -> (NOT p)`. Worked verification: all 4 assignments agree — **True**. The converse `q -> p` is NOT equivalent (check p=T,q=F: implication false, converse true). Practical use: to prove 'if the build passes then tests ran', prove the contrapositive 'if tests did not run then the build fails' — often the easier direction. Confusing implication with converse is one of the most common logic errors in specifications.

notes.title: Predicate logic over finite domains
notes.body: Predicates add quantifiers: `FORALL x, P(x)` and `EXISTS x, P(x)`. Over a finite domain you can evaluate them by enumeration. Worked example: domain = {2, 3, 4}, statement `EXISTS x, x is prime AND x > 3`. Check: x=2 (prime, not >3, fails), x=3 (prime, not >3, fails), x=4 (not prime, fails). No witness exists, so the statement is **false**. Change `>3` to `>=3`: x=3 is prime and >= 3, so the statement becomes **true**. Existence claims need exactly one witness; universal claims need every case. This discipline maps directly onto testing: 'there exists an input that crashes' vs 'for all inputs it terminates'.

notes.title: Boolean algebra for systems work
notes.body: Boolean algebra gives simplification laws: absorption `p OR (p AND q) = p`, distribution, idempotence `p AND p = p`. Worked example: simplify `(admin AND active) OR (admin AND NOT active)`. Factor admin: `admin AND (active OR NOT active)` = `admin AND T` = **admin**. Verified by enumerating all 4 assignments of (admin, active): both sides agree on every row. Why it matters: access-policy engines evaluate exactly these expressions. Simplifying before deploying means fewer rules, faster evaluation, and policies a human can audit. Firewall rules, SELinux booleans, and access policies are boolean expressions; simplify them with these laws.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **filesystem hierarchy** — the map of a Linux system: /etc holds configuration, /var holds variable data (logs, spool), /usr holds programs and libraries, /home holds user data, /proc and /sys are kernel interfaces, not real files.
- **permissions** — the law: rwx across user/group/other, expressed as octal (640 = rw-r-----), plus setuid/setgid/sticky bits (4755 = setuid + rwxr-xr-x: executes with the file owner's privileges).
- **pipes** — connect a command's stdout to the next command's stdin (|): the instrument you think in, as in journalctl ... | grep -i error | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr — filter, extract, count, rank.
- **redirection** — send output to files: > overwrites, >> appends.
- **text processing** — grep, sed, awk, sort, uniq, xargs: the toolkit for turning log noise into answers.
- **set -euo pipefail** — the three lines that prevent 3 AM pages: exit on error (-e), on undefined variables (-u), and on pipe failures (-o pipefail). In every script.
- **users/groups/ACLs** — useradd and groupmod manage identity; setfacl/getfacl grant fine-grained access beyond owner/group/other.
- **systemd** — the init and service manager: units with [Unit]/[Service]/[Install] sections, systemctl enable --now to enable and start, journalctl -u to read a service's logs, targets and timers (timers are the modern cron: calendar or monotonic triggers with journal logging).
- **LVM** — the layer that makes resizing sane: physical volumes (PV, the disks) pour into a volume group (VG, the pool); logical volumes (LV) are sliced out. Resize any layer independently; also Stratis, Btrfs, and VDO (deduplication/compression) as the storage alternatives.
- **firewalld** — zone-based firewalling: assign interfaces to zones, open services not ports (--add-service=http), rich rules for exceptions.
- **ip / nmcli / ss** — the modern networking tools: ip replaces ifconfig, nmcli manages NetworkManager, ss -tlnp shows TCP listening sockets with numeric ports and the owning process.
- **SELinux** — mandatory access control by context (user:role:type:level): a file can have correct Unix permissions and still be denied because its context is wrong. ls -Z shows contexts, restorecon repairs them, semanage fcontext persists the rule, audit2allow generates policy (use sparingly — understand the denial before allowing it).
- **podman** — daemonless, rootless container runtime: the RHEL-native tool (quadlets integrate containers with systemd as services).
- **RHCSA (EX200)** — Red Hat's hands-on performance exam: broken systems and a clock, man pages available; it recycles the same five root causes (service running? port listening? firewall? SELinux? disk full?).

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Do this on a lab VM or with loop devices — never on a machine you care about. The procedure builds the full LVM lifecycle and grows the filesystem online, then writes a hardening audit script.

1. Create a file-backed 'disk' so the lab is safe anywhere: dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256, then DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img).
2. Build the LVM layers in order: pvcreate "$DEV", then vgcreate vgdata "$DEV", then lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata.
3. Put a filesystem on it and mount it: mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/applv, mkdir -p /mnt/app, mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app; confirm with df -h /mnt/app.
4. Extend online with zero downtime: lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv, then xfs_growfs /mnt/app (or resize2fs for ext4). Confirm the new size with df -h.
5. Clean up in reverse: umount, lvremove, vgremove, pvremove, losetup -d.
6. Write the hardening audit script starting every script with set -euo pipefail: grep -R NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ for passwordless sudo, find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002 for world-writable files, ss -tlnp for listening ports, and journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -ci 'failed' for today's failed SSH logins; write all findings to a dated report file.
7. Create an SELinux trap on purpose: move a file from /home to /srv/web, confirm ls -Z shows the wrong context, then restorecon -Rv /srv/web and confirm the service can read it again. This is the exam's favorite trap — rehearse it until it is boring.

dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)

mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vgdata/applv && mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app

restorecon -Rv /srv/web          # fix the context

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Systems administration is a discipline of verification. In Linux Foundations to RHCSA, these habits separate operators from outage-causers:
- **Running commands you cannot explain.** Especially as root. Before Enter, say what the command does, what it changes, and how you would undo it.
- **Changing production without a way back.** Snapshot, backup, or config copy first — every time. 'It should be fine' is not a rollback plan.
- **Ignoring the logs.** The system is telling you what happened. `journalctl`, event viewer, and service logs come before hypotheses, not after.

- **Documenting nothing.** Future-you is a stranger. Every change in Linux Foundations to RHCSA gets: what, why, the exact command, and how you verified it worked.
- **Testing only the happy path.** Reboot it. Break the network. Kill the service. Systems fail; your job is knowing they recover.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **NTFS permissions** — file-system rights (Full Control, Modify, Read & Execute, List Folder Contents, Read, Write, plus special permissions like Traverse and Execute File): they travel with the file and form the real security boundary.
- **share permissions** — the network entry point's rights: they combine with NTFS, and the effective access is the *most restrictive* of the two. This single rule answers half the permissions questions.
- **effective access** — compute it, don't guess it: the Effective Access tab shows the real result; guessing permissions is how outages happen.
- **services** — background processes managed via services.msc, sc.exe, or PowerShell Get-Service: startup types, dependencies, and recovery actions.
- **registry** — the configuration database (e.g. HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services): export before editing, always.
- **event logs** — Event Viewer (System/Application/Security), wevtutil, Reliability Monitor: troubleshooting starts here. Methodology: reproduce, check logs, isolate, fix, verify, document.
- **Server Core vs Desktop Experience** — Core is the smaller attack surface with fewer patches: the exam's preferred answer for a new server, fully manageable remotely.
- **forest** — the Active Directory security boundary; contains domains, which contain OUs. Design OUs by *administration*, not by org chart.
- **Group Policy** — GPOs link to sites, domains, and OUs; processing order is LSDOU (Local, Site, Domain, OU — later wins); Enforced beats Block Inheritance. gpupdate /force applies now, gpresult /r shows what applied.
- **AGDLP** — the canonical group-nesting pattern: Accounts go into Global groups, into Domain Local groups, which get the Permissions.
- **Kerberos** — ticket-based authentication (AS then TGS then service): needs time sync (more than ~5 minutes of skew kills auth), registered SPNs, and a reachable KDC — the troubleshooting trio.
- **NTLM** — legacy challenge-response authentication: pass-the-hash risk, avoid where Kerberos works.
- **hybrid identity** — Entra ID Connect syncs on-prem AD with Entra ID for SSO shapes across cloud and on-prem.
- **PowerShell pipeline** — passes *objects*, not text: Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5. Filter left (Where-Object early), format right (Format-* last — formatting destroys the objects).
- **PowerShell remoting / DSC** — Enter-PSSession and Invoke-Command run code on remote machines; DSC is the declarative configuration model (desired state, LCM enforces it).
- **DNS** — zones, records, forwarders, scavenging: internal resolution working but external failing points at forwarders or root hints first.
- **DHCP** — scopes, reservations, failover: the DORA dance (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge); the classic 80/20 scope split is legacy thinking — proper failover is the modern answer.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Do this on a lab Server Core VM with the AD DS role — the procedure rehearses the three skills the module keeps testing: permissions reasoning, GPO scoping, and pipeline discipline.

1. Create a folder C:\Share\Finance, set NTFS Modify for the Finance group and share Read for the same group; then open the Effective Access tab for a Finance user and record the result: Read — most restrictive wins. Widen the share to Change and re-check.
2. Build the OU design: one OU per administration boundary (e.g. OU=Workstations,OU=Sales), never one OU per org-chart box. Link a GPO at the domain level and a conflicting setting at the OU level.
3. Run gpresult /r on a test client and read which GPO won the conflict: the OU-linked one (LSDOU — later wins). Then set Enforced on the domain GPO and re-check the flip.
4. Break Kerberos on purpose: skew the client clock by 8 minutes and attempt a domain logon; confirm failure. Sync with w32tm, confirm logon works. You now own the most-tested Windows troubleshooting fact there is.
5. Write a PowerShell audit one-liner and save it as a script (no aliases in scripts): Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} | Sort-Object DisplayName | Select-Object Name, Status — filter left, format right.
6. Use Invoke-Command to run the audit against two lab machines at once: remoting is how one admin covers a fleet.
7. Document every change you made (GPO links, share/NTFS settings, clock skew) with a rollback note — documented change is the discipline, not the paperwork.

gpresult /r

# Pipeline discipline: filter left, format right

# One audit, many machines
Invoke-Command -ComputerName SRV1,SRV2 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} }

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **OSI model** — seven layers (physical → data link → network → transport → session → presentation → application): the troubleshooting map. Isolate bottom-up — cabling before configuration.
- **TCP/IP model** — the four-layer working model the Internet actually runs on; OSI is the map, TCP/IP is the territory.
- **IPv4 / CIDR** — dotted-decimal addresses with prefix lengths: /24 = 254 hosts, /27 = 30 hosts, hosts = 2^(32-n) − 2.
- **IPv6** — hex addresses with prefix lengths; no broadcast (multicast instead); link-local fe80::/10, global unicast, and subnetting on nibble boundaries (/48 site, /64 subnet) — easier than v4 once the hex clicks.
- **subnetting** — borrowing host bits to carve networks: the 60-second drill (given any /25–/28, produce network/broadcast/usable range) is trainable and tested.
- **VLSM** — variable-length subnet masks: right-size each subnet (point-to-point links get /30 or /31, VLANs get what they need) instead of wasting a /24 on two routers.
- **summarization** — aggregating contiguous blocks (192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.3.0/24 → 192.168.0.0/22): smaller routing tables, valid when the blocks are contiguous with the same next hop.
- **VLAN** — virtual LAN: segments broadcast domains on one switch fabric.
- **802.1Q** — the VLAN tagging standard: trunk ports carry tagged frames for multiple VLANs; access ports carry one untagged VLAN.
- **STP** — Spanning Tree Protocol: loop prevention. A port in blocking state is listening, not forwarding — that is the protocol working, not a failure.
- **OSPF** — link-state routing inside one autonomous system: Dijkstra's algorithm, areas, fast convergence.
- **BGP** — path-vector, the Internet's routing protocol: carries policy between autonomous systems (AS_PATH in concept). Different job from OSPF — interior speed vs exterior policy.
- **802.11 / wireless** — a/b/g/n/ac/ax across 2.4/5/6 GHz with MIMO and channel width; on 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, 11 don't overlap — the most-tested wireless fact in existence.
- **WPA2 vs WPA3** — WPA3's SAE handshake replaces the crackable WPA2 4-way handshake and resists offline dictionary attacks.
- **firewall** — stateful vs NGFW (next-generation, application-aware): the policy enforcement point.
- **load balancer** — distributes traffic across servers (algorithms: round-robin, least-connections).
- **proxy / IDS/IPS** — proxies mediate and cache; IDS detects, IPS prevents — placement determines what they can see.
- **SNMP / NetFlow/sFlow** — monitoring: SNMP polls device state, NetFlow/sFlow sample traffic. You can't troubleshoot what you don't measure — baselines first, anomaly detection second.
- **Wireshark** — the packet analyzer: follow a TCP stream, read the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), spot retransmissions (congestion or loss), decode DNS and DHCP exchanges, recognize the TLS ClientHello.
- **6-step troubleshooting methodology** — identify the problem, establish a theory, test the theory, establish a plan, implement, verify and document. Same discipline as the scenarios: scope first (one host? one VLAN? everyone?), then bottom-up.
- **PBQ** — performance-based questions: Network+ sims for subnetting, CLI-output analysis, and diagram troubleshooting. The drill set rehearses exactly these; the objective weights say troubleshooting (24%) comes first.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Two drills, daily for two weeks. This is arithmetic reflex and packet reading — both are trained, not studied.

1. Subnetting drill: take 192.168.20.64/27. Host bits = 5, so 32 addresses: .64–.95. Network .64, broadcast .95, usable .65–.94. Do one random /25–/28 per day and time yourself; under 60 seconds is the target.
2. Summarization drill: take 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.3.0/24 — four contiguous /24s share 22 network bits → 10.1.0.0/22. Say the rule out loud: contiguous blocks, same next hop.
3. Open Wireshark on your lab interface and capture while you open one web page. Stop the capture.
4. Find the TCP three-way handshake: filter tcp.flags.syn==1, confirm the SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence to the web server's port 443. That sequence is the most-read pattern in packet analysis.
5. Right-click one TCP packet and choose Follow → TCP Stream. Read the TLS ClientHello — the moment encryption negotiation begins.
6. Run a DHCP exchange (ipconfig /release then /renew on Windows, or restart networking on Linux) while capturing: identify the DORA sequence — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — four packets, in order.
7. Introduce loss on purpose (unplug for two seconds mid-transfer, or throttle the lab link) and watch retransmissions appear: retransmissions mean segments went unacknowledged — loss, congestion, or a dead peer.
8. Apply the 6-step methodology to one real lab fault per week: identify (scope: one host? one VLAN? everyone?), theory, test, plan, implement, verify/document. Write the one-paragraph postmortem.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your applied capstone for this module: a network design document and a troubleshooting playbook for a small company — the two artifacts that prove you can both build and fix.

The scenario. A 60-person company is moving into a two-floor office: wired workstations, a small server room, warehouse scanners on Wi-Fi, and a guest network that must never touch the corporate LAN. Their current 'network' is one flat /24 and a consumer router.

Your deliverables:
- The addressing plan: VLSM design with right-sized subnets per VLAN (workstations, servers, voice, warehouse Wi-Fi, guest, and /30 or /31 point-to-point links), plus the summarized route you would advertise upstream — every subnet justified, no wasted space.
- The switching design: VLAN assignments, which ports are access vs 802.1Q trunk, where STP is protecting you, and the channel plan for the 2.4 GHz warehouse coverage (1/6/11, with the reasoning).
- The routing call: where static routes suffice and where a dynamic protocol earns its keep — OSPF inside, and the one-paragraph explanation of what BGP would be for if they ever multi-home.
- The security layer: firewall placement and policy sketch, where IDS/IPS sits, WPA3 for corporate wireless with the SAE rationale, and the guest segmentation that keeps visitors off the LAN.
- The troubleshooting playbook: the 6-step methodology written as a runbook ('the network is down' → scope first: one host? one VLAN? everyone?), the Wireshark capture procedure with the three patterns to check first (handshake, DNS, DHCP), and the monitoring baseline (what SNMP/NetFlow would collect so the next fault has something to compare against).

Stretch: produce the summarized supernet for a second site and show the single route entry that covers both.

notes.body:
**Problem.** 192.168.20.64/27 — usable range?

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** .65–.94
- **Why:** /27: 32 addresses, .64–.95; network .64, broadcast .95; usable .65–.94. Covered in the Hands-on procedure section.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: */27: 32 addresses, .64–.95; network .64, broadcast .95; usable .65–.94.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Systems administration is a discipline of verification. In Networking Core: Network+, these habits separate operators from outage-causers:
- **Running commands you cannot explain.** Especially as root. Before Enter, say what the command does, what it changes, and how you would undo it.
- **Changing production without a way back.** Snapshot, backup, or config copy first — every time. 'It should be fine' is not a rollback plan.
- **Ignoring the logs.** The system is telling you what happened. `journalctl`, event viewer, and service logs come before hypotheses, not after.
- **Firewall/SELinux whack-a-mole.** Disabling the security layer to 'make it work' masks the real misconfiguration. Diagnose the denial; write the correct rule or context.
- **Documenting nothing.** Future-you is a stranger. Every change in Networking Core: Network+ gets: what, why, the exact command, and how you verified it worked.
- **Testing only the happy path.** Reboot it. Break the network. Kill the service. Systems fail; your job is knowing they recover.

modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3 of IL-04 — Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks. I'm your instructor, and this module is the network itself: the Network+ N10-009 core with Wireshark-level packet literacy. We start with the maps — the OSI and TCP/IP models, IPv4 and IPv6 addressing — then build the reflex every network engineer owns: subnetting to the point where a /27 is arithmetic, not a puzzle. From there: switching and VLANs, routing protocols, wireless, the appliances that sit in the path, and finally the skill that separates engineers from guessers — reading packets and applying the 6-step troubleshooting methodology with evidence. The Network+ exam leans on performance-based questions; this module rehearses exactly those, and the packet work you do here will serve every role you ever take after it.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **inventory** — the list of managed hosts: INI or YAML, organized into groups; the exam starts here, so a wrong inventory fails everything downstream.
- **patterns** — host selection expressions: webservers:&staging intersects, webservers:!staging excludes, --limit narrows a run to one host for iteration.
- **playbook / play / task / module** — a playbook is a YAML list of plays; a play maps tasks onto hosts; a task calls a module. Ad-hoc first (ansible web -m ping) to prove the concept, then write the playbook.
- **variables and facts** — variables parameterize playbooks (extra vars with -e win every precedence fight); ansible_facts (e.g. ansible_facts['os_family']) describe the target for when: conditionals — one playbook, many distributions.
- **Jinja2** — the templating language inside playbooks: when: already evaluates Jinja2, so never double-wrap {{ }} inside a when: clause.
- **idempotence** — running twice changes nothing the second time: the *definition* of correct automation. Every task must be safe to re-run — state: present, never shell commands that append blindly.
- **handlers** — tasks that run once at the end of a play, only when notified by a changed task (notify: restart nginx): restart the service only when the config changed.
- **ansible-vault** — encrypts secrets at rest in the repo; decrypt at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or a vault password file. Never commit plaintext credentials.
- **roles** — reusable automation units with a conventional layout (tasks/main.yml, handlers/main.yml, templates/, defaults/main.yml): learn the layout once, reuse forever.
- **Galaxy** — the community sharing hub for roles: vet what you download.
- **RHEL system roles** — Red Hat's supported roles (timesync, selinux, firewall, storage, network): idempotent and tested — prefer them over hand-rolled or random Galaxy roles on the exam.
- **automation controller** — the enterprise scheduling and access layer over Ansible: know at concept level what a job template bundles (project + inventory + credentials + playbook), plus workflows and RBAC.
- **become** — privilege escalation done right: become: true on the play or task that needs root on the remotes.
- **EX294** — the RHCE performance exam: real RHEL systems and a clock, configured with Ansible to a specification. YAML indentation, Jinja2 quoting in when:, and a forgotten become: true are the common traps; --check --diff is the pre-flight for every run.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Build the idempotent web tier from the module lab, then prove idempotence — the proof is the grade.

1. Write the inventory first: a [web] group with your lab hosts. Run ansible web -m ping and confirm every host answers before writing a single task.
2. Skeleton the playbook before filling tasks: play name, hosts: web, become: true, empty tasks and handlers blocks, variable file if you need one. Structure first, logic second — this is the exam time-saver.
3. Add the package task with ansible.builtin.dnf: name=nginx, state=present. Declarative state, not shell commands.
4. Add the config task with ansible.builtin.template: src=index.html.j2, dest with mode '0644', and notify: restart nginx — the handler fires only when the template actually changes.
5. Add the firewall task with ansible.posix.firewalld: service=http, permanent=true, immediate=true, state=enabled. Services, not raw ports — same discipline as Module 1.
6. Add the service task with ansible.builtin.service: name=nginx, state=started, enabled=true.
7. Pre-flight: ansible-playbook web.yml --check --diff --limit web1 — the dry run shows what WOULD change, on one host.
8. Run for real: ansible-playbook web.yml. Then run it again immediately: the second run must report 0 changed. Zero changes on re-run is idempotence proven — that is the verdict you want.
9. Break it on purpose: change one line in the template, re-run, and confirm the handler fires exactly once and only the config task reports changed.
notes.code:
---
- name: web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: nginx installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nginx
        state: present
    - name: index deployed
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: index.html.j2
        dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
        mode: '0644'
      notify: restart nginx
    - name: http allowed
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        service: http
        permanent: true
        immediate: true
        state: enabled
    - name: nginx running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true
  handlers:
    - name: restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
# prove it:
ansible-playbook web.yml --check --diff --limit web1
ansible-playbook web.yml && ansible-playbook web.yml  # second run: 0 changed

notes.body:
Your applied capstone for this module: a timed, multi-system automation engagement — the closest rehearsal to EX294 short of the exam itself.

The scenario. A company has four RHEL systems fresh off the Module 1 build procedure and a specification document: two web servers behind one load-balancer config, one database server with a tuned config, and one monitoring host collecting logs — all to be brought to spec with Ansible, nothing by hand.

Your deliverables:
- The inventory with groups (web, db, monitor) and group variables; ad-hoc proof (ansible all -m ping) captured before any playbook ran.
- One playbook per tier, each starting from the skeleton-first pattern, using become: true where privilege is needed, handlers for every service restart, and when: conditionals on ansible_facts where the tiers diverge.
- At least one RHEL system role used where it fits (timesync across all four hosts is the natural one) instead of a hand-rolled equivalent — with the written reason.
- Secrets handled with ansible-vault (the database password), with the vault password file outside the repo and the encryption proven by showing the ciphertext in version control.
- The idempotence proof: two consecutive full runs with the second reporting 0 changed, plus the --check --diff pre-flight output for the final run.
- A time-boxed run log: you get one 90-minute window to go from empty repo to green second run — log start/end times and where the minutes went, because the exam is a workday compressed.

Stretch: convert the most-reused tier into a proper role (tasks/handlers/templates/defaults layout) and consume it from a thin wrapper playbook.

notes.title: Worked example: A task using shell: echo x >> /etc/motd is ___.
notes.body:
**Problem.** A task using shell: echo x >> /etc/motd is ___.

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** not idempotent — appends on every run
- **Why:** >> appends every run — use copy/template with content: for idempotence. Covered in the Concepts section.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *>> appends every run — use copy/template with content: for idempotence.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

notes.title: Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Systems administration is a discipline of verification. In RHCE: Ansible Automation, these habits separate operators from outage-causers:
- **Running commands you cannot explain.** Especially as root. Before Enter, say what the command does, what it changes, and how you would undo it.
- **Changing production without a way back.** Snapshot, backup, or config copy first — every time. 'It should be fine' is not a rollback plan.
- **Ignoring the logs.** The system is telling you what happened. `journalctl`, event viewer, and service logs come before hypotheses, not after.
- **Firewall/SELinux whack-a-mole.** Disabling the security layer to 'make it work' masks the real misconfiguration. Diagnose the denial; write the correct rule or context.
- **Documenting nothing.** Future-you is a stranger. Every change in RHCE: Ansible Automation gets: what, why, the exact command, and how you verified it worked.
- **Testing only the happy path.** Reboot it. Break the network. Kill the service. Systems fail; your job is knowing they recover.

scriptLabs.title: LVM: Build, Extend, Grow — Online
scriptLabs.brief: Script the full LVM lifecycle: PV → VG → LV → filesystem → extend → online grow. Use loop devices so it's safe anywhere. Required fragments force the layer order.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# Use a file-backed loop device as our 'disk'
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
echo "disk: $DEV"
# YOUR TASK: pvcreate, vgcreate vgdata, lvcreate -n applv -L 100M, mkfs.xfs, mount, then extend + xfs_growfs
scriptLabs.hint: pvcreate $DEV && vgcreate vgdata $DEV && lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata && mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/applv. Extend: lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv && xfs_growfs /mnt/app.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
pvcreate "$DEV"
vgcreate vgdata "$DEV"
lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata
mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vgdata/applv
mkdir -p /mnt/app && mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app
df -h /mnt/app
# online extend: no unmount, no downtime
lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv
xfs_growfs /mnt/app
df -h /mnt/app
# cleanup: umount /mnt/app; lvremove -y /dev/vgdata/applv; vgremove -y vgdata; pvremove -y $DEV; losetup -d $DEV

scriptLabs.title: Bash Hardening Audit Script
scriptLabs.brief: Write an audit script with set -euo pipefail that checks: passwordless sudo entries, world-writable files in /etc, listening ports without a known service, and failed SSH logins today. Output a findings report.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
REPORT=/tmp/audit-$(date +%F).txt
{
echo "=== hardening audit $(date) ==="
# YOUR TASK 1: sudoers without password (visudo -c friendly: grep NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers*)
# YOUR TASK 2: world-writable under /etc
# YOUR TASK 3: listening TCP ports (ss -tlnp)
# YOUR TASK 4: failed SSH logins today (journalctl)
} > "$REPORT"
echo "wrote $REPORT"
scriptLabs.hint: grep -R NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/. find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002. journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -i 'failed'.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
REPORT=/tmp/audit-$(date +%F).txt
{
echo "=== hardening audit $(date) ==="
echo '--- NOPASSWD sudoers ---'
grep -R --include='*' 'NOPASSWD' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ 2>/dev/null || echo 'none found'
echo '--- world-writable in /etc ---'
find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -print 2>/dev/null || echo 'none found'
echo '--- listening TCP ---'
ss -tlnp
echo '--- failed SSH today ---'
journalctl -u sshd --since today 2>/dev/null | grep -ci 'failed' || echo 0
} > "$REPORT"
echo "wrote $REPORT"

scriptLabs.title: Ansible: Idempotent Web Tier
scriptLabs.brief: Write a playbook that installs nginx, deploys a templated index.html, opens the firewall, and enables the service — fully idempotent, with a handler. Then prove idempotence with a second run.
scriptLabs.starter:
---
- name: web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    # YOUR TASK: nginx present, index.html from template, firewalld http, service enabled+started, notify handler on template change
  handlers:
    # YOUR TASK: restart nginx
scriptLabs.hint: Use ansible.builtin.yum/dnf with state: present; template src -> dest notify: restart nginx; firewalld service=http permanent+immediate; service state=started enabled=true.
scriptLabs.solution:
---
- name: web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: nginx installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nginx
        state: present
    - name: index deployed
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: index.html.j2
        dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
        mode: '0644'
      notify: restart nginx
    - name: http allowed
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        service: http
        permanent: true
        immediate: true
        state: enabled
    - name: nginx running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true
  handlers:
    - name: restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
# prove it: ansible-playbook web.yml && ansible-playbook web.yml  # second run: 0 changed

answerBank.q: How do I beat SELinux instead of disabling it?
answerBank.a: Learn the three commands: ls -Z (see the context), restorecon (fix file contexts), semanage fcontext (persist the rule). Disabling SELinux on the exam fails the task; in production it removes a layer. The module's labs make contexts routine.

answerBank.q: NTFS or share permissions — which do I set?
answerBank.a: Both, deliberately: NTFS for the real security boundary (it travels with the file), share for the network entry point. Effective access is the most restrictive of the two — design with that rule, verify with the Effective Access tab.

answerBank.q: How do I get fast at subnetting?
answerBank.a: The 60-second drill in the trainer: random /25–/28, produce network/broadcast/usable range. Daily for two weeks. It's arithmetic reflex, not intelligence — everyone who practices gets fast.

answerBank.q: Wireshark feels overwhelming — where to start?
answerBank.a: Three patterns: the TCP handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK), DNS query/response, DHCP DORA. Follow one TCP stream per session. The module's packet notes build from these three outward.

Microsoft's directory service: domains, forests, OUs, Group Policy, Kerberos auth — the Windows identity plane.
Centralized Windows configuration management; applied in LSDOU order with Enforced/Block Inheritance overrides.
File-level access control on Windows; effective access = most restrictive of NTFS and share permissions.
Domain Name System: hierarchical name→IP resolution; A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV records.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: automatic IP assignment via DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Ack).
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK: how TCP establishes a reliable connection before data flows.
Recording raw frames (Wireshark/tcpdump) for evidence-based troubleshooting — 'trust, but verify on the wire'.
Seven-layer networking reference (Physical→Application); the troubleshooting map: isolate the failing layer.
Agentless automation via SSH/WinRM: YAML playbooks of idempotent tasks, organized into roles.
firewalld/iptables grouping of interfaces with per-zone rules; default-deny posture with explicit allows.
The Bourne-Again Shell: interactive command line and scripting language — the Linux admin's primary tool.

faq.a: They're complementary, not sequential: RHCSA proves you can run Linux, Network+ proves you understand the wire. The course runs Linux first (modules 3) then networks (module 5) because packet literacy lands better once you can drive the endpoints.

faq.q: Do I need physical hardware for the labs?
faq.a: No. A hypervisor (Hyper-V, VirtualBox, KVM) plus evaluation ISOs for Windows Server and a RHEL-like distro covers everything. The course notes RAM/CPU minimums per lab.

faq.q: Why Ansible for RHCE instead of shell scripts?
faq.a: EX294 tests Ansible specifically — and idempotent, declarative automation is the industry direction. Shell scripts are covered in Linux Foundations; RHCE is the automation proof.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-27 (IT Infrastructure Specialist)?
faq.a: IL-04 is the systems/networking *foundation* (RHCSA/RHCE, Windows Server, Network+). IL-27 builds on it toward the ThreatLocker-facing infrastructure specialist role with Zero Trust, Intune, and interview prep. Take IL-04 first.

faq.q: I broke my VM networking. Where do I start?
faq.a: Bottom-up: `ip a` (link up? address present?) → `ip r` (default route?) → ping gateway → ping 8.8.8.8 → ping name (DNS?). The packet-literacy cheat sheet is the checklist.

faq.q: SELinux keeps blocking my lab. Should I disable it?
faq.a: No — disabling it is the exam-wrong answer and the production-wrong answer. Learn `ls -Z`, `restorecon`, and `audit2why`. The drills deliberately train this reflex.

faq.q: Windows or Linux focus for jobs?
faq.a: Both — that's the point of the course. Enterprise estates are hybrid: AD + Entra on the identity side, Linux on the workload side. Single-OS admins compete for half the roles.

faq.q: How do the performance exams differ from multiple choice?
faq.a: EX200/EX294 give you live VMs and tasks ('configure X so that Y works') — no partial credit for recognizing the answer. The course's timed hands-on scenarios simulate exactly that.
